results.content: doi: 10.1007/s10508-020-01650-w Reproducibility and Registration in Sexuality Research ### Tierney K Lorenz 1 Department of Psychology and Center for Brain, Biology and Behavior, University of Nebraska–Lincoln, Lincoln, NE 68588 Find articles by Tierney K Lorenz 1 Department of Psychology and Center for Brain, Biology and Behavior, University of Nebraska–Lincoln, Lincoln, NE 68588 Email: Tierney.lorenz@unl.edu PMCID: PMC7046084 NIHMSID: NIHMS1558020 PMID: 32030577 The publisher's version of this article is available at Arch Sex Behav Most readers of the _Archives of Sexual Behavior_ will by now be familiar with an upsurge of interest in best practices for reproducibility and replicability across modern scientific disciplines (Ioannidis, 2005; National Academies of Sciences Engineering and Medicine, 2019; Simmons, Nelson, & Simonsohn, 2011). In sex research, issues with reproducibility most typically arise when there is poor access to the original data or lack of transparency in reporting on the analytic method (rather than being a function of complex processes introducing non-systematic error, as in experimental physics). Pre-registration is a process by which researchers clearly describe the details of their research plan, including methods and analysis decisions, _prior to conducting the research._ A key element of pre-registration is the publication or cataloging of the (preliminary) research plan in a publicly accessible format that provides time-stamped evidence of when the plan was established. Issues with Data Analysis and Data Sharing Preregistration is not necessary in all research designs (e.g., for exploratory work), but transparency in one’s research decisions, and open sharing of data and materials will always be critical for good science. One final minor note on transparency issues specific to sex research: I urge those of us who regularly use psychophysiological assessments of sexual response to either use published methods for data cleaning (e.g., Prause, Williams, & Bosworth, 2010; Pulverman, Meston, & Hixon, 2018) or to fully document the many, many decisions that occur when cleaning and condensing psychophysiology data and presenting these as an online appendix. confirmatory analyses, (2) making available all (de-identified) materials and data in public repositories with meta-data, (3) clearly describing decisions regarding data cleaning and statistical testing, (4) appropriately qualifying interpretations of results from individual studies, and (5) proactively seeking out and addressing one’s own biases in the conduct of sexuality research.

results.title: How to Improve Transparency and Reproducibility in Decision Analysis
results.content: # What are the best tools and techniques to improve transparency and reproducibility in decision analysis? In this article, you will learn about some of the best tools and techniques to improve transparency and reproducibility in decision analysis. One of the most important steps to improve transparency and reproducibility in decision analysis is to document your assumptions. Absolutely, documenting assumptions is a cornerstone for transparency and reproducibility in decision analysis. Documenting assumptions is crucial for enhancing transparency and reproducibility in decision analysis. This documentation can be done using text, tables, diagrams, or code comments, serving as a valuable reference point for yourself and others to assess the validity and reliability of the decision analysis. Another way to improve transparency and reproducibility in decision analysis is to use open source software. Using open source software will help you to ensure the quality and integrity of your decision analysis, and to foster a culture of openness and collaboration. Utilizing open-source software can significantly enhance transparency and reproducibility in decision analysis. A third way to improve transparency and reproducibility in decision analysis is to apply good coding practices. Applying good coding practices will help you to avoid errors and bugs in your decision analysis, and to make your code more reusable and adaptable. Employing good coding practices is essential for bolstering transparency and reproducibility in decision analysis. A fourth way to improve transparency and reproducibility in decision analysis is to create interactive dashboards. Interactive dashboards can play a pivotal role in enhancing transparency and reproducibility in decision analysis. By visualizing data, models, and results in an interactive format, dashboards provide a user-friendly interface for exploring and understanding the decision-making process. A fifth way to improve transparency and reproducibility in decision analysis is to conduct sensitivity analysis. Sensitivity analysis is a powerful tool for enhancing transparency and reproducibility in decision analysis. A sixth way to improve transparency and reproducibility in decision analysis is to document your workflow. You can also use tools like R Markdown, Jupyter Notebook, or Knitr to create dynamic documents that integrate your code, data, and results. Documenting your workflow will help you to organize and manage your decision analysis, and to share and reproduce your work.

results.title: Navigating PROSPERO4animals: 10 top tips for efficient pre-registration of your animal systematic review protocol - PMC
results.content: # Navigating PROSPERO4animals: 10 top tips for efficient pre-registration of your animal systematic review protocol. Pre-registering a systematic review protocol has several benefits, including avoiding unplanned duplication of reviews, reducing reporting biases, and providing structure throughout the review process. PROSPERO4animals is the international prospective register of systematic reviews (PROSPERO) for the preregistration of systematic review of animal studies. These tips address common difficulties that both beginners and experienced researchers may face when pre-registering their systematic review protocols. This article aims to help authors write and register a detailed systematic review protocol on PROSPERO4animals. **Keywords:** Systematic review, Preclinical research, Meta-research, Methodology, Pre-registration, Transparency. The international prospective register of systematic reviews (PROSPERO; [5]) is an online platform that facilitates pre-registration of your systematic review protocol. 2018) is the sub-section of this register dedicated to protocols of systematic reviews of animal studies. To facilitate the process, we hereby provide 10 top tips to speedy pre-registration in PROSPERO4animals, the dedicated register for animal systematic review protocols. If this is the first time you are conducting a systematic review or meta-analysis, please include methodological experts (e.g., an information specialist and a meta-analysis expert) in your review team to improve the quality of your work. Prospectively registering systematic review protocols helps to reduce potential reporting biases, avoid duplication of research efforts, and increases transparency [12]. We strongly recommend assessing the internal validity (risk of bias) of the included studies using the SYstematic Review Centre for Laboratory animal Experimentation (SYRCLE) risk of bias tool [15], or a study quality assessment tool [16] tailored to animal studies (see Appendix 1). Writing and registering your PROSPERO4animals protocol will help you to identify possible hurdles in your planned methodology at the start of your systematic review process. For further methodological and educational resources on the planning and conduct of systematic reviews of animal studies, please refer to the references and links provided in Tip #1. By following these 10 tips, authors can navigate common difficulties in completing a registration in PROSPERO4animals, speed up the registration process, and improve the quality, transparency, and reproducibility of their systematic review. results.content: ## SC20 Is Everywhere We Are. Home Submit Transparency and Reproducibility Initiative. # Transparency and Reproducibility Initiative. SC has been a leader in tangible progress towards scientific rigor, through its pioneering practice of enhanced reproducibility of accepted papers. SC20 sees the initiative expanded to encompass transparency and reproducibility for the broader objective of enhanced scientific rigor, and streamlined for reduced researcher burden. Transparency of research results is achieved by papers that, for instance, provide evidence for why one algorithm worked and others do not, or provide evidence of a rigorous criteria having been followed to choose one software architecture over another. Author attention to enhancing the transparency of their science methodologies is a complement to reproducibility details in strengthening the overall rigor of a scientific publication. **The SC20 Transparency and Reproducibility Initiative impacts technical papers and their submission and peer review in the following ways:**. * The Artifact Description (AD) Appendix will be auto-generated from author responses to a standard form embedded in the online submission system. ### Transparency and Reproducibility Initiative Evaluation.

Distinguished Professor of Economics, Oxfam Professor in Environmental and Resource Economics, & Faculty co-Director of the Center for Effective Global Action (CEGA). # Edward Miguel. ###### Research. # Transparency, Reproducibility, and the Credibility of Economics Research. Christensen, Garret S., and Edward Miguel. "Transparency, Reproducibility, and the Credibility of Economics Research", *Journal of Economic Literature*, 56(3): 920-980. There is growing interest in enhancing research transparency and reproducibility in economics and other scientific fields. We survey existing work on these topics within economics, and discuss the evidence suggesting that publication bias, inability to replicate, and specification searching remain widespread in the discipline. We next discuss recent progress in this area, including through improved research design, study registration and pre-analysis plans, disclosure standards, and open sharing of data and materials, drawing on experiences in both economics and other social sciences.
